Beyond Smart School Buildings: Investing in Learning, Teachers and Every Child.
T H E  S I T U A T I O N
Education is the foundation of human development, economic productivity and social progress. The quality of an
education system should therefore be measured not by the number or cost of school buildings constructed, but by
the quality of teaching, what children actually learn and the opportunities education creates for their future.
48: The Peter Mbah administration’s Smart Green School Initiative is presented as a flagship programme designed to
modernise education in Enugu State through the construction of new, technology-enabled school infrastructure.
However, the promise of modern education is increasingly being undermined by serious concerns about the quality,
location and execution of several of these projects. Reports of poorly constructed facilities, inadequate quality
assurance, defective and reportedly collapsing structures raise fundamental questions about the standards of
supervision, contractor accountability and the value delivered for public funds. Even more troubling is the apparent
disconnect between school locations and the communities they are meant to serve, with some facilities reportedly
situated several kilometres away from the children expected to attend them. A school that is structurally unsafe,
poorly located or inaccessible to its intended pupils cannot be presented as educational transformation. Modern
education is not measured by impressive buildings or political announcements, but by safe, functional and
accessible learning environments that genuinely improve children’s access to quality education.
A modern school without qualified teachers cannot deliver quality education. Computers without trained teachers,
reliable electricity and maintenance arrangements may become expensive unused assets. Equally, children in rural
communities should not be disadvantaged because they live far from newly constructed model schools.
O U R  O B J E C T I V E S
An NDC government will pursue a learning-centred and inclusive education policy with the following objectives:
1 Improve learning outcomes 2 Strengthen existing public schools
3 Improve teacher quality and welfare 4 Ensure equitable access
5 Make Smart Green Schools sustainable 6 Promote practical and relevant education
7 Strengthen accountability
S T R A T E G I C  P R O G R A M M E S
A.  Smart Green Schools Audit, Completion and Sustainability Programme
Within its first 100 days, an NDC government will initiate an independent technical, financial and educational audit of the
Smart Green Schools programme. The audit will establish the status of completed and incomplete projects, verify
expenditure and contractual obligations, assess construction quality and identify the recurring costs of operating and
maintaining the facilities.
Useful infrastructure will be preserved, viable projects completed and identified defects corrected. Any established
financial irregularities will be referred to the appropriate authorities. Future investments will be guided by educational
needs, affordability and demonstrated value for money rather than political visibility.
B.  Existing Public Schools Rehabilitation Programme
The government will undertake a statewide assessment of existing primary and secondary schools and introduce a phased
rehabilitation programme. Priority will be given to unsafe classrooms, dilapidated buildings, inadequate desks, insufficient
toilets, lack of clean water and shortages of essential teaching and learning materials. Rehabilitation will be guided by
transparent budgets, implementation timelines and public reporting. Every community deserves access to a functional
public school, whether or not it hosts a Smart Green School.
49: C.  Foundational Learning and Educational Excellence Programme
The NDC will introduce a statewide literacy and numeracy intervention to ensure that children acquire the basic skills
necessary for successful learning. Baseline assessments will identify pupils experiencing learning difficulties, while
remedial teaching, appropriate instructional materials and regular assessments will help address learning gaps.
Educational performance will be measured through independently assessed literacy and numeracy levels, attendance,
retention and completion rates, rather than simply the number of schools commissioned or computers purchased.
D.  Teacher Recruitment, Development and Welfare Programme
Teachers are the foundation of quality education. The government will assess staffing shortages, recruit qualified teachers
according to verified requirements and strengthen professional development. Priority interventions will include timely
payment of salaries, transparent promotion procedures, improved working conditions and continuous training in literacy,
numeracy, science, classroom management and appropriate digital teaching methods.
E.  Equitable Access and Inclusive Education Programme
The NDC will assess school distances, rural accessibility, transportation requirements and barriers facing children with
disabilities. Existing community schools that remain educationally viable will be maintained and improved. School
consolidation will only be considered where evidence demonstrates educational benefits without imposing unreasonable
travel burdens on children. Targeted interventions will address the needs of disadvantaged households and communities
with limited educational opportunities.
F.  Digital Learning, Science and Technology Programme
The NDC supports the use of technology, science laboratories, robotics and digital learning where they demonstrably
improve educational outcomes. However, procurement must be justified by educational needs and supported by teacher
training, reliable power supply, maintenance arrangements and sustainable operating budgets. Technology will
complement effective classroom instruction, not replace qualified teachers or become an avenue for wasteful expenditure.
G.  School Feeding, Pupil Welfare and Practical Skills Programme
Subject to a sustainable funding framework, the government will strengthen school feeding and essential pupil welfare,
prioritising disadvantaged communities. Transparent procurement and independent monitoring will safeguard public
resources. Schools will progressively expand practical education in agriculture, science, digital literacy, technical skills,
entrepreneurship and the creative arts. These interventions will equip young people with relevant knowledge and practical
competencies for further education, employment and self-reliance.
4.  Funding, Implementation and Accountability
The NDC will develop a costed medium-term education financing plan based on verified needs, available revenue and
existing contractual commitments. Expenditure will prioritise essential recurrent obligations, teacher welfare, foundational
learning, school rehabilitation and sustainable infrastructure. During the first six months, government will establish
baseline information on school infrastructure, teacher availability, pupil enrolment and literacy and numeracy levels.
Urgent safety repairs will be identified, alongside a phased rehabilitation and financing plan.
50: During the first year, priority interventions will address critical infrastructure deficiencies, teacher shortages and
foundational learning gaps. Over the four-year administration, investments will progressively improve existing schools,
strengthen teacher development and expand practical and digital learning. An annual public education scorecard will
report progress in literacy, numeracy, school attendance, teacher availability, school safety, infrastructure rehabilitation and
expenditure accountability. Specific performance targets will be established following the baseline assessment.

Water for All: Solar-for-Water
24-Month Programme for Sustainable Pipe-Borne Water Supply.
T H E  S I T U A T I O N
Access to clean, affordable and reliable pipe-borne water remains a major challenge for residents of Enugu State.
Despite the existence of major water sources and treatment facilities, including Ajali, Oji River and Iva Valley,
successive administrations have failed to ensure a consistent supply of treated water to households, markets and
communities. Consequently, thousands of households depend on commercial water tankers, private boreholes and
other alternative sources, often at considerable financial cost. Some households reportedly spend between ₦20,000
and ₦40,000 monthly purchasing water from commercial suppliers. Three major challenges account for this
persistent failure:
1.  Inadequate Water Infrastructure and Limited Distribution Networks
Existing water facilities do not adequately serve many expanding urban settlements, new layouts and rural
communities. Several neighbourhoods remain outside the reach of the existing pipe network. Communities in
Nkanu, Udenu and other parts of the state also require the development of additional reliable water sources.
2.  Excessive Dependence on Electricity and Diesel
Water treatment and distribution require substantial electricity to operate pumping machines. Dependence on
unreliable national grid electricity and expensive diesel-powered generators increases production costs and makes
continuous water supply difficult. Whenever electricity fails or funds for diesel become unavailable, pumping
stations shut down and water supply is interrupted.
3.  Neglect of Existing Infrastructure and Poor Maintenance
Several reservoirs, pumping stations and distribution pipelines have deteriorated because of inadequate
maintenance and poor management. Some existing elevated storage reservoirs, which could support gravity-based
water distribution, are either underutilised or in need of rehabilitation. The consequence is that residents are forced
51: to spend additional money purchasing water, while the government continues to bear the financial burden of
operating inefficient water facilities. An NDC Government will change this situation through a practical
combination of solar energy, rehabilitation of existing infrastructure, development of additional water sources, new
distribution pipelines and community-based water facilities.
Our approach will be to reduce the cost of water production, improve distribution efficiency and expand access to
clean water without imposing additional taxes on residents.
O U R  O B J E C T I V E S
The NDC Government’s WATER FOR ALL: SOLAR-FOR-WATER programme will pursue the following objectives:
1 Restore reliable public water supply 2 Achieve substantial coverage within 24 months
3 Reduce water production costs 4 Expand water infrastructure
5 Develop additional water sources 6 Provide affordable and safe drinking water
7 Eliminate preventable water-related diseases 8 Protect citizens from additional taxation
S T R A T E G I C  P R O G R A M M E S
The NDC Government will implement the WATER FOR ALL: SOLAR-FOR-WATER programme through the following strategic
interventions:
1.  Solar-Power the Major Water Treatment and Pumping Stations
Rather than spending billions of naira constructing entirely new treatment plants where existing facilities can be
rehabilitated, government will prioritise the modernisation of existing major water infrastructure.
The Action:
Install industrial-scale solar photovoltaic systems at major water treatment and pumping stations, including Ajali, Oji River
and other operational facilities.
The solar installations will be designed to support the energy requirements of heavy-duty water pumps and treatment
equipment.
How It Will Work:
During daylight hours, solar energy will power water treatment and pumping operations, substantially reducing
dependence on the national electricity grid and diesel generators.
Where necessary, appropriate battery storage and grid or backup-power arrangements will ensure continuity of essential
operations beyond daylight hours.
The result will be lower operating costs, fewer interruptions and a more reliable water supply system.
2.  Rehabilitate and Reactivate Community Storage Reservoirs
Water must not only be treated and pumped; it must also be stored strategically to ensure reliable distribution.
The Action:
Government will undertake a comprehensive technical assessment, rehabilitation, cleaning and restoration of existing
elevated storage reservoirs across the state.
52: Priority will be given to reservoirs at Abor, Udi, Trans-Ekulu, New Haven and other strategic locations, subject to
engineering assessments.
How It Will Work:
Solar-powered pumping systems will move treated water from the treatment facilities into elevated community reservoirs
during the day.
These reservoirs will provide strategic storage capacity, ensuring that water remains available for distribution even when
pumping operations are temporarily interrupted.
This will reduce pressure on pumping infrastructure and improve the reliability of the distribution system.
3.  Expand Pipe Networks and Construct New Storage Facilities
A major weakness of the existing water system is that several new residential layouts and expanding communities are not
adequately connected to public water infrastructure.
The Action:
Government will embark on a phased expansion of water distribution pipelines and the construction of additional storage
tanks in underserved areas.
Priority will be given to new residential layouts, densely populated neighbourhoods, markets and communities that have
historically been excluded from public water supply.
The programme will also address gaps in the existing network so that newly developed areas are not left dependent on
expensive private water suppliers.
How It Will Work:
New transmission and distribution pipelines will connect existing treatment facilities and rehabilitated reservoirs to
neighbourhoods and residential streets.
The expansion will be based on a comprehensive water infrastructure master plan identifying existing coverage, population
growth, demand and areas requiring new infrastructure.
4.  Introduce Gravity-Based Water Distribution
One of the most cost-effective ways of distributing water is to take advantage of natural elevation.
The Action:
Government will maximise the use of elevated reservoirs and strategically located storage tanks to distribute treated water
through natural gravity.
How It Will Work:
Once water has been pumped into elevated reservoirs, gravity will provide the pressure required to move water through
appropriately designed distribution pipelines to surrounding neighbourhoods.
This will reduce the need for continuous electricity-powered pumping at every stage of distribution, lower operating
expenses and improve system efficiency.
Where terrain or distance makes gravity distribution inadequate, appropriately designed booster pumping stations will be
installed.
53: 5.  Establish Solar-Powered Rural Water Schemes
Access to reliable pipe-borne water must not be restricted to Enugu metropolis and major urban centres.
The Action:
Government will introduce decentralised Solar Water Kiosks in rural communities that cannot immediately be connected
to central water distribution networks.
These facilities will consist of properly constructed boreholes, solar-powered pumping systems, elevated storage tanks and
community water collection points.
How It Will Work:
Solar panels will power borehole pumps to fill elevated storage tanks during daylight hours.
Treated and tested water will then be made available through designated community collection points.
Each facility will have a designated maintenance arrangement, trained local operators and a sustainable funding
mechanism to ensure that equipment is maintained and water remains affordable.
No community will be abandoned to unsafe water sources because it is too far from the main distribution network.
6.  Finance the Programme Without Additional Taxes
The NDC Government will pursue a financing model that protects ordinary residents from additional taxation while
mobilising the resources required for this major infrastructure programme.
The proposed financing strategy will include:
A.  Coal-for-Infrastructure Partnership
Enugu State possesses significant coal deposits. Government will explore transparent and legally compliant partnerships
with qualified mining and infrastructure investors.
Under an appropriately structured agreement, investors may undertake specified solar infrastructure development in
exchange for legally permissible mining rights and other agreed commercial benefits.
Such arrangements must undergo independent valuation, environmental assessment, competitive procurement and
legislative oversight where required.
The state’s mineral resources must generate measurable public benefits rather than become another source of waste or
exploitation.
B.  International Green Energy and Climate Grants
The programme will seek grants and concessional financing from international development institutions and climate-
finance programmes.
Potential partners will include the African Development Bank and other institutions supporting renewable energy, water
security and climate-resilient infrastructure.
The government will prepare bankable project proposals to attract grant support for solar equipment, pumping systems
and water infrastructure.
54: The target will be to maximise grant financing and minimise the debt burden on the state. Any proposed grant percentage
will depend on actual programme eligibility and approved funding agreements.
C.  Eliminate Government Financial Waste
Government will strengthen the Treasury Single Account (TSA), improve revenue collection and enforce financial discipline
across ministries, departments and agencies. Savings from reduced administrative waste, unnecessary expenditure and
poorly prioritised projects will be redirected towards essential water infrastructure.
D.  Public-Private Infrastructure Partnerships
Where appropriate, government will engage competent private-sector operators under transparent performance-based
contracts for the construction, operation and maintenance of water infrastructure.
All partnerships will protect public ownership of essential water assets and guarantee affordability, accountability and
quality standards.
The ultimate objective is to make clean, safe and affordable public water accessible to a substantial proportion of Enugu
residents within the first two years of the NDC administration.
